issues.legal_issue: A second appellate court may not reappreciate concurrent factual findings unless a substantial question of law arises, such as where those findings are perverse or affected by non-reading or misreading of evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that the plaintiff owned the property, relying on oral and documentary evidence.
The second appellate court framed questions that assumed the property belonged to the temple, although the lower courts had found otherwise.
The second appellate court reassessed the evidence and reversed the concurrent findings without identifying perversity, non-reading, or misreading of evidence.
issues.conclusion: The second appellate court exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Its judgment was set aside and the concurrent findings were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal lies only on a substantial question of law. A High Court should not reassess evidence or interfere with concurrent findings of fact unless they are perverse or affected by non-reading or misreading of evidence. The substantial questions must arise from the findings actually made, not from an assumed fact contrary to those findings.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and no_perversity_or_evidentiary_misreading and questions_assume_facts_contrary_to_findings

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from a lower court's decision.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual findings after evaluating the evidence.
predicates.no_perversity_or_evidentiary_misreading: The findings are not shown to be perverse or to result from evidence being ignored or misunderstood.
predicates.questions_assume_facts_contrary_to_findi: The questions framed for the second appeal proceed on factual assumptions inconsistent with the lower courts' findings.

issues.definition: When a second appeal presents concurrent factual findings without perversity or evidentiary misreading, and the framed questions assume contrary facts, the second appellate court cannot reverse those findings.

issues.legal_issue: An objection that concerns only the mode of proving an otherwise admissible document must be raised when the document is tendered, or it is waived.
material_facts: Photocopies of a public order and a rent agreement were admitted in evidence and marked as exhibits without objection.
The opposing parties challenged the photocopies in the second appeal because the originals had not been produced and, as to the rent agreement, because the copy was said to be unreadable.
The tenant admitted signing the rent agreement, and the plaintiff explained why the certified copy of the public order was not available in the proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The later objections concerned the mode of proof and could not be raised after the documents had been admitted without timely objection. The second appellate court erred in excluding the documents.
issues.legal_principle: Order 13 Rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for the court's endorsement when a document is admitted in evidence. An objection that a document is itself inadmissible may still be raised later, but an objection only to an irregular or insufficient mode of proof must be made when the document is tendered. If a timely objection could have allowed the party tendering the document to cure the defect, failure to object waives the need for formal proof. This distinction is supported by Padman v. Hanwanta, P.C. Purushothama Reddiar v. S. Perumal, and the rule discussed in The Roman Catholic Mission v. The State of Madras.

rule.if: civil_evidence_proceeding and document_itself_admissible and objection_only_to_proof_method and no_timely_objection

predicates.civil_evidence_proceeding: The dispute involves documents tendered as evidence in a civil proceeding.
predicates.document_itself_admissible: The document is of a kind that is admissible in evidence, rather than being barred from evidence altogether.
predicates.objection_only_to_proof_method: The objection concerns how the document was proved, such as the use of a copy, rather than the document's inherent admissibility.
predicates.no_timely_objection: The opposing party did not object when the document was tendered and admitted.

issues.definition: If an admissible document is challenged only as to its method of proof and no timely objection is made, the objection is waived.

issues.legal_issue: Regularly kept account-book entries relating to a matter in dispute are relevant evidence, and the absence of supporting day books or testimony from a deceased maker does not by itself justify excluding them.
material_facts: The plaintiff produced annual ledger books kept by his father and later by the plaintiff, recording rent received from the tenant.
The plaintiff testified that the books were regularly maintained and submitted to the income tax authorities; the books bore the department's seal.
The testimony about the books and their regular maintenance was not challenged in cross-examination.
The lower courts accepted the books and found that the entries supported the plaintiff's claim to have collected rent as landlord.
issues.conclusion: The account books should not have been excluded from consideration merely because supporting day books were not produced or the deceased father who made some entries did not testify.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes entries in books of account regularly kept in the course of business relevant when they refer to a matter the court must inquire into. Under Section 32(2), statements made by a deceased person in the ordinary course of business, including entries in regularly kept books, are relevant. Depending on the circumstances, a court may require corroboration before acting on an entry; in this case the lower courts were entitled to rely on the entries and the plaintiff's testimony.

rule.if: civil_proceeding and accounts_regularly_kept and entries_relate_to_disputed_matter and regularity_and_authenticity_unchallenged

predicates.civil_proceeding: The issue arises in a civil proceeding in which the court must evaluate documentary evidence.
predicates.accounts_regularly_kept: A party maintained the account books regularly in the ordinary course of business.
predicates.entries_relate_to_disputed_matter: The entries concern a matter the court must decide, such as the receipt of rent relevant to the claimed landlord relationship.
predicates.regularity_and_authenticity_unchallenged: The evidence of regular maintenance and authenticity was not challenged by the opposing party.

issues.definition: Regularly kept account entries concerning a disputed matter cannot be excluded merely because day books or testimony from a deceased maker are absent when their regularity and authenticity are unchallenged.

issues.legal_issue: In a civil suit for possession based on title, a plaintiff who creates a high degree of probability in favour of title shifts the onus to the defendant, and the plaintiff's burden is discharged if the defendant does not shift the onus back.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought possession on the basis of ownership and relied on rent records, account books, a rent agreement, tax records, and other evidence of possession through a tenant.
The temple produced no evidence establishing its title to the property.
The trial court and first appellate court found that the plaintiff's evidence created a high degree of probability of title and that the temple had not discharged the onus shifted to it.
The second appellate court reassessed the evidence despite those findings.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff's evidence was sufficient to shift the onus to the temple, and the temple's failure to discharge that onus meant the plaintiff's burden of proving title was met.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 defines when a fact is proved; in civil proceedings, proof is assessed on a preponderance of probabilities, not beyond reasonable doubt. As explained in A. Raghavamma v. Chenchamma, the burden of proof remains on the party asserting a fact, while the onus of proof may shift during the evaluation of evidence. In a title-based possession suit, a high degree of probability supporting the plaintiff's title can shift the onus to the defendant; if the defendant does not shift it back, the plaintiff's burden is treated as discharged. Brahma Nand Puri v. Neki Puri states that the plaintiff must succeed on the strength of the title established, not merely on the weakness of the defendant's title.

predicates.title_based_possession_suit: The plaintiff seeks possession of property on the basis of an asserted title.
predicates.plaintiff_evidence_creates_high_probabil: The plaintiff's evidence makes it highly probable that the plaintiff holds title to the property.
predicates.defendant_fails_to_discharge_shifted_onu: After the evidence shifts the onus to the defendant, the defendant does not produce evidence sufficient to shift it back.

issues.definition: In a title-based possession suit, highly probative evidence of the plaintiff's title discharges the plaintiff's burden if the defendant does not meet the shifted onus.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot, while the tenancy continues, deny the title of the landlord who inducted the tenant or validly attorn to another claimant as landlord.
material_facts: The plaintiff and his father had inducted the tenant and collected rent from him over a period of years.
While that tenancy was continuing, the tenant began paying rent to the temple and executed a rent note in its favour.
The temple's claim of ownership had failed in the relevant administrative proceeding, and it produced no other evidence establishing title.
The tenant's agreement in favour of the plaintiff and the account books supported the plaintiff's position as landlord.
issues.conclusion: The tenant's attornment to the temple was invalid, and the estoppel under Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act operated against the tenant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 estops a tenant from denying that the landlord had title to the property at the beginning of the tenancy. A tenant inducted by a landlord cannot, during the continuance of the tenancy, treat another claimant as landlord in a manner that denies the original landlord's title.

rule.if: tenant_landlord_dispute and landlord_inducted_tenant and tenancy_continues and tenant_attorns_to_competing_claimant

predicates.tenant_landlord_dispute: The proceeding concerns competing claims to the landlord-tenant relationship over property.
predicates.landlord_inducted_tenant: The claimant seeking to enforce the tenancy was the person who inducted the tenant or succeeded to that landlord's position.
predicates.tenancy_continues: The tenancy remains in force when the tenant takes the disputed step.
predicates.tenant_attorns_to_competing_claimant: The tenant recognizes a competing claimant as landlord while the existing tenancy continues.

issues.definition: When a landlord inducted a tenant and the tenancy continues, the tenant's attornment to a competing claimant is barred by the tenant's inability to deny the original landlord's title.

issues.legal_issue: Entries in municipal tax records do not establish title, although they may evidence tax liability or, depending on the governing scheme and surrounding circumstances, possession.
material_facts: The municipal records identified the plaintiff and his predecessors in the ownership column, and the plaintiff produced property-tax payment records.
The temple's name was not entered in the municipal records before the dispute arose.
The temple relied on its later collection of rent and payment of property tax, but those records arose after the dispute had developed.
The temple produced no other evidence establishing its title.
issues.conclusion: The municipal entries did not themselves prove title, but the long-standing entries and tax payments were relevant to show who was treated by the municipality as liable for the taxes and could support an inference concerning possession. The temple's later entries and payments did not establish its title.
issues.legal_principle: A municipal assessment or tax entry is not, by itself, evidence of ownership. Depending on the scope of the governing provision, it may show who was treated as liable for rates and taxes and may evidence possession. Entries over time and related tax payments may be considered with other evidence, but do not substitute for proof of title.

predicates.property_title_dispute: The proceeding requires the court to determine ownership of property.
predicates.municipal_records_are_relied_on_as_owner: A party relies on municipal assessment or tax records to support a claim of ownership.

issues.definition: In a property title dispute, reliance on municipal assessment or tax records as proof of ownership does not establish title, though such records may bear on tax liability or possession.

issues.legal_issue: An administrative decision made without jurisdiction to determine title to immovable property is not itself proof of title, but may be relevant to show the competing claim made and how that claim was resolved in the administrative proceeding.
material_facts: An Assistant Commissioner issued an order in a proceeding under the religious and charitable endowments legislation, finding that the temple was not the owner of the disputed property.
The order was tendered as a photocopy of a certified copy and admitted without objection.
The plaintiff explained that the certified copy was in the record of another proceeding.

The court recognized that the administrative authority could not adjudicate title to immovable property, while treating the decision as relevant to the temple's claim and its failure in that proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The administrative order was not evidence conclusively determining civil title, but it was relevant to show the temple's claim and that the claim had failed in that proceeding. The copy could not be excluded for its mode of proof after it had been admitted without objection.
issues.legal_principle: An administrative authority lacking legal competence to adjudicate title to immovable property cannot determine civil title. A public order and its certified copy may be admissible to prove the order's existence and contents, and the order may be relevant to the history and outcome of a claim. Under the rule stated in the judgment, a mode-of-proof objection to an otherwise admissible document must be made when the document is tendered; failure to do so waives that objection.

predicates.administrative_order_in_evidence: A party tenders an order made by an administrative authority as evidence in a property dispute.
predicates.authority_lacks_jurisdiction_to_determin: The authority that made the order is not legally empowered to decide title to the immovable property.
predicates.order_relates_to_competing_ownership_cla: The order concerns a claim by one party that the property belongs to it.

issues.definition: An administrative order concerning a competing ownership claim may show how that claim was dealt with, but it does not conclusively establish title when the authority lacked power to decide title.
